labour_share.label: Compensation of employees as a share of GDP
labour_share.note: Computed here as 100 x DTWM / YBHA (both current prices, annual; YBHA from source ons_ybha), rounded to one decimal place. Excludes the labour income of the self-employed (mixed income), so it is lower than labour-share measures that adjust for self-employment.

The same table gives 1.3% as the OBR's 2025 outturn; the later ONS estimate (IHYP) differs, so the two are not spliced.

business_ai_use.label: Businesses using at least one AI technology, all sizes
business_ai_use.note: Business Insights and Conditions Survey, private-sector businesses in the industries BICS covers (it excludes, among others, agriculture, finance and insurance, and public administration), weighted by count of businesses. Survey question: "Which of the following artificial intelligence technologies, if any, does your business currently use?" Options: Autonomous vehicles; Data processing using machine learning; Image processing using machine learning; Robotics; Text generation using Large Language Models; Visual content creation; Other (Please describe); Not sure; Business does not currently use artificial intelligence technologies. Dates are the midpoint of each wave.

workers_high_exposure_high_complementari.label: Workers in occupations with high AI exposure and high complementarity
workers_high_exposure_high_complementari.note: IMF estimates as reported by DSIT/AISI. DSIT: the IMF measures exposure using an index of the correspondence between AI applications and the human abilities each occupation requires; its complementarity assessment is based on the social and physical context of work, and in high-complementarity roles AI may be more likely to boost efficiency and productivity. DSIT notes such indices are indicative rather than precise. The two high-exposure groups sum to 67%; the DSIT text says 'around 70%'.

notes: Official published data only; no PolicyEngine modelling. The OBR series is the OBR's own forecast.

Labour Force Survey quality: in its October 2026 labour market bulletin (https://www.ons.gov.uk/employmentandlabourmarket/peopleinwork/employmentandemployeetypes/bulletins/uklabourmarket/october2026) the ONS says LFS response has improved and is now close to its pre-pandemic level, but that some volatility remains, particularly in estimates for mid-2023 and throughout 2024 and in detailed breakdowns with small samples, and advises users to focus on long-term movements rather than short-term changes. LFS estimates are official statistics; the ONS has told the Office for Statistics Regulation it will not seek reaccreditation for them and is prioritising the Transformed LFS as their replacement.
LFS rolling three-month estimates are labelled in ONS files by their middle month; periods here are given as the full three months.
GDP and productivity figures are revised as new data arrive; values are as published on the release dates in 'sources'.
The OBR October 2026 EFO gives 2025 GDP growth of 1.3% (its outturn at the time); the ONS series IHYP, released 12 November 2026, gives 1.2%. The difference is a data vintage, not a forecast.
Compensation of employees as a share of GDP is the only computed series (a ratio of two ONS series); it is not the ONS's self-employment-adjusted labour share.

Exposure by SOC major group is null: the DfE report 'The impact of AI on UK jobs and training' (November 2023) publishes AIOE scores only for 4-digit SOC 2010 unit groups with no major-group table or employment counts, and no later DfE/DSIT source with SOC 2020 major-group scores was found. Aggregating the unit-group scores ourselves (for example an unweighted mean by major group) is possible but would be our own construction on SOC 2010.
BICS covers private-sector businesses in selected industries; results for businesses with 0 to 9 employees carry large survey weights, so the ONS often headlines the 10-or-more-employees figure.
